thread.title: Institutional Investors Already Bailed | Seeking Alpha

author: Kwan-Chen Ma
title: Institutional Investors Already Bailed | Seeking Alpha
text:
By K C Ma and Bilal Hashmi
We like to watch how and when institutions trade. Unlike retail investors, institutional investors rely more on fundamentals and less on sentiments to make investments decisions. One way to observe how institutions trade, with a time lag, is through the changes of their holding on each stock, which is reported in the quarterly 13F filings. In working with recent institutional ownership data, we noticed a striking pattern in institutional trading, which has not been revealed by any writing as we know, in the early part of 2018. In this post, we would like to provide some conjectures for this pattern.
FAANG Stocks To start with, in Figure 1A, we show the institutional holding on the most watched FAANG stocks, including Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ), and Google- ) for the past 1 year. It should be fairly easy for your eyes to catch the strikingly similar "hump" of the institutional holding across all five stocks. Apparently, institutions have increased their investments in the FAANG stocks approximately around 10-15% in early February and decreased by 10-15% in early May. The more interesting part is the seeming close coordination of the purchase and sale decisions across all institutions. It is also important to note that the increase and decrease in holding were rather significant in size. Both similarities suggest the changes in institutional holding may be driven by some common macro events. We will delay our conjecture about what macro events may have caused this common change in the later section after we illustrate how pervasive this pattern is. In the following sections, we will examine how prevalent this pattern has been for the rest of the market.
Technology Stocks In Figure 1B, we present the institutional holding, over the same time period of five major technology stocks, including Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ), Oracle (NYSE: ORCL ), Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA ), and Micron (NASDAQ: MU ). It is pretty clear that major technology stocks exhibit virtually the same pattern of institutional ownership changes in both magnitude and timing.
Automobile Stocks We also present additional evidence on the three major automobile stocks, including General Motors (NYSE: GM ), Ford (NYSE: F ), and Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ). The inclusion of automobile stocks reflects several unpleasant realities. U.S. automobile stocks are the first victims of both the U.S. aluminum and steel tariffs and China's retaliation tariffs on U.S. cars. If the tariffs or trade war were an institutional motive to trade, we should see a similar pattern in institutional ownership changes around the time of tariffs announcements. In fact, we do in Figure 1C.
Financial Stocks There is a stylized argument that the downturn of the 2018 stock market has been mainly driven by the Fed's tightening or raising interest rates. Although we are not looking at the stock prices per se in this post, rising interest rates could be a good reason that motivated institutions to change their positions. From this angle, in Figure 1D, we present the institutional holding changes of four major financial stocks, including Bank of America (NYSE: BAC ), Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC ), Citi Group (NYSE: C ), and Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS ). The purpose of examining these stocks is to provide contrasting evidence. If rising interest rates, which will help financial stocks, were driving the stock market, institutional investors should have not reduced their holding in the financial stocks. In fact, they did.
Commodity Stocks Since we have a "hunch" that the pattern may have something to do with the economic outlook, we decided to look at the most cyclical sector. In Figure 1E, we present the institutional holding, over the same time period of four major commodity stocks, including U.S. Steel (NYSE: X ), Toll Brothers (NYSE: TOL ), Lowe's (NYSE: LOW ), and Archer Daniels Midland (NYSE: ADM ). These stocks cover basic metal, housing, material and commodity industries which are more sensitive to the future business cycle. Do you see the same pattern in Figure 1E?
Retail Stocks In 2018, we would have been in denial if we did not consider the potential impact of tariffs or trade war. Since the most recent tariffs have been targeted to $200 billion retail goods and the prospect of a trade war leading into a global recession is real, in Figure 1F, we examine the four major retail stocks, including Starbucks (NASDAQ: SBUX ), Target (NYSE: TGT ), Nike (NYSE: NKE ), and Darden (NYSE: DRI ). The retail stocks are either directly affected by the tariffs or indirectly affected by the likelihood of a future recession. In all cases, we see the familiar pattern again.
U.S. Tax Cut From the last 24 graphs, it is clear that institutional investors have simultaneously increased their investments in major U.S. stocks and subsequently reduced their holding by almost the same amount within the next three months. There should be little disagreement why institutions increased their investments around the turn of 2018. The timing seems to coincide with the passage of the U.S. tax cut. (Note: The 13Fs filing tends to lag the actual trading about 30-45 days.)
Rising Interesting Rates? On the other hand, there are several stylized arguments to explain why institutional investors reduced their investment significantly after late March (filed around early May). The first that came to our minds is because the Fed has been aggressively raising interest rates which will slow down the economy. While this may be a likely reason, it seems inconsistent with the evidence above. For one, the Fed has raised eight times of Fed Fund rates since 2015. It is hard to imagine what new rate moves would have "spooked" the institutions to simultaneously to decide to exit around March. Second, you would think that financial stocks will welcome the idea of rate increases, but the institutional investors dumped the four financial stocks, just like the rest of the pack. In other words, institutions may reduce their holding across the board because of the fear of future recession. But the fear was not generated by the rate hikes then.
Institutions Smelled the Recession Fear If you read this far into this post, we ask your further indulgence to entertain our most likely conjecture. Talking about tariffs or trade war is inevitably politically sensitive. But the impact of tariffs and trade war is undeniably widespread and significant. For the case of targeted tariffs, the initial direct cost impact may be "mitigated" by effectively supply chain management. However, for the more recent across-the-board tariffs on the $200 billion-plus China import goods, Walmart (NYSE: WMT ) and Target have already warned that the tariffs will have to be eventually passed to the consumers.
While the tariffs-induced cost increase may be inflationary, the real fear is on the demand impact from the escalated trade war. Admit or not, we are in the midst of a global trade war. The timing or the extent of the trade war may be delayed or negotiated, but the damage cannot be avoided. With tariffs cost increase and near-embargo product flow, the global demand for goods and services will have to be reduced. That is the definition of a global recession. It appears that institutions have picked up the clue back in March when the first sign of a trade war surfaced. At this point, there is no evidence that institutional money has returned.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AMZN, NVDA. it (other than from Seeking Alpha).
